newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin strengthens reformers, govt calls for calm.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin strengthens reformers, govt calls for calm.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin named more liberal reformers to his government on Wednesday in the final stage of a long reshuffle that fell on the eve of planned nationwide protests over the state of the Russian economy.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin repeated a well-worn pledge to start paying off billions of dollars in overdue wages and pensions -- the main source of discontent -- and to create economic growth.
But with the nation's patience wearing thin, he appealed for more time and made a plea for calm on the planned day of action.
"We mustn't get carried away by emotion and provocation," he said. "Such problems are not solved by demonstrations."
"We will do everything we can to resolve them," Chernomyrdin told a news conference after meeting Yeltsin to map the way forward and approve the latest cabinet appointees.

Yeltsin himself, in a radio address mainly devoted to defending the outcome of his Helsinki summit last week with U.S. President Bill Clinton, said he was satisfied with the reshuffle he initiated three weeks ago and hoped it would deliver results.

"The line-up is interesting. Strong. Now that just has to be confirmed in deeds," he said. It was a classic Yeltsin statement, combining a vote of confidence with a reminder that the president keeps himself aloof from the government's record.
Chernomyrdin's last government lasted less than nine months, although the premier has been in office since December 1992.
During his news conference, he was flanked by youthful and reformist new first deputy prime minsters, Anatoly Chubais, 41, and Boris Nemtsov, 37. Both took office earlier this month.

Keeping up the liberal tone of the reshuffle, Chernomyrdin said ex-economy minister Yevgeny Yasin, the guiding spirit of many economic reforms, would keep a government job as minister without portfolio, coordinating and reviewing economic policy.
Alexei Kudrin, a Chubais ally, became First Deputy Finance Minister. Chubais himself holds the finance portfolio.
Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, who is also a deputy prime minister, kept his job, which includes day-to-day responsibility for customs and tax inspection.

Keeping the conservative Kulikov may be a slight setback for Chubais. But it was balanced by giving reformist deputy premier Alfred Kokh control of customs and tax policy and by naming Kudrin, under Chubais, to overall charge of revenue raising.
The new cabinet's main and immediate target is to bring about economic growth and revive investment, Chernomyrdin said.
"This is the task already for the current year," he said, stressing the need to begin radical structural reforms among companies, natural monopolies, housing and welfare.

In an effort to calm spirits, Chernomyrdin promised that the state and private employers would pay 11.8 trillion roubles ($2 billion) in back wages and pensions in March. The government puts total arrears at 53 trillion roubles.
It was not clear where the money would come from.
He stressed that tax collection was still the government's biggest headache and said sweeping reform of tax and budget policy was needed to keep state finances from seizing up.
Nemtsov said Yeltsin was determined to cut government spending. Former governor of the Nizhny Novgorod carmaking region, he said the state would no longer buy foreign cars.

Chernomyrdin said he was aware of some plans to disrupt peaceful protests. The government has put security services on the alert. Trade unions say 20 million could turn out, although previous protests have failed to fire popular enthusiasm.
The leader of the extreme communist faction, Working Russia, forecast a "quiet and peaceful" day. Viktor Anpilov was quoted urging his supporters not to provoke disturbances.

Yeltsin, 66, returned to active politics this month after eight months of illness. He acknowledged market reforms were failing to meet people's needs and hopes the new team can free the economy from a web of corruption, crime and bureaucracy.
